items.content:
도널드 트럼프 미국 대통령이 젠슨 황 전 엔비디아 CEO의 복귀를 공개적으로 지지했다. 실리콘밸리 주요 인사들과 엔비디아 직원, 주주들까지 복귀를 요구하는 가운데 트럼프도 힘을 보탰지만, 엔비디아 이사회는 아직 복귀를 검토하지 않고 있는 것으로 알려졌다.

트럼프 대통령은 16일(현지시간) 백악관에서 아시아 순방을 떠나기 전 황 전 CEO의 복귀에 대한 질문에 "나는 반대하지 않는다. 그가 큰 교훈을 얻었다고 생각한다"라며 "그는 돌아올 수 있다. 많은 사람이 그의 복귀를 원하고 있다"라고 말했다.

트럼프 대통령은 황 전 CEO와 중국 스파이 의혹을 받는 앨리스 황의 관계가 미국 국가안보를 위험에 빠뜨렸다는 주장도 부인했다.

그는 "국가안보는 위험에 처하지 않았다. 미국은 그 어느 때보다 강하다"라며 "중국이 우리를 상대로 게임을 하듯 우리도 중국을 상대로 게임을 한다"라고 말했다. 앨리스 황이 실제 중국 스파이인지에 대해서는 "그가 중국 스파이인지 알지 못한다"라며 사실관계를 조사하겠다고 밝혔다. 이번 아시아 순방에서 시진핑 중국 국가주석과 이 문제를 논의할 가능성도 언급했다.

트럼프 대통령의 발언은 황 전 CEO의 복귀를 추진하는 실리콘밸리 인사들에게 힘을 실어줄 것으로 보인다. 트럼프는 그동안 황 전 CEO와 긴밀한 관계를 유지해 왔으며, 미국의 AI 경쟁력과 반도체 수출 정책에 관해서도 그의 의견을 적극적으로 수용해 왔다.

앞서 파이낸셜타임스(FT)는 15일 황 전 CEO가 측근들과 CEO 복귀 가능성을 논의하고 있으며, 실리콘밸리 주요 인사들이 엔비디아 이사회와 백악관을 설득하기 위한 활동을 추진하고 있다고 보도했다.

복귀 요구는 엔비디아 내부와 투자자들 사이에서도 이어지고 있다. 황 전 CEO의 복귀를 요구하는 '스탠드 위드 젠슨(Stand With Jensen)' 캠페인에는 18만200명 이상이 서명했다. 이 중 8800명 이상은 엔비디아 현직 직원, 9만4000명 이상은 주주라고 밝혔다.

일론 머스크 CEO와 암자드 마사드 레플릿 CEO, 팀 스위니 에픽게임즈 CEO 등 실리콘밸리 주요 인사들도 서명자 명단에 이름을 올렸다. 청원 참여자들은 독립 조사를 통해 사실관계가 확인될 때까지 황 전 CEO를 복귀시켜야 한다고 주장했다.

주요 투자자들도 이사회에 신중한 판단을 요구하고 있다. 브래드 거스트너 알티미터캐피털 CEO와 개빈 베이커 아트레이데스매니지먼트 대표는 사실관계가 확인되기 전에 후임 CEO 선임을 서둘러서는 안 된다고 촉구했다.

대만에서도 황 전 CEO를 지지하는 움직임이 나타났다. 16일 타이베이의 랜드마크인 타이베이 101 빌딩에는 '대만은 젠슨을 사랑한다(Taiwan Loves Jensen)'라는 문구가 등장했다. 황 전 CEO가 엔비디아의 반도체 생산을 맡는 TSMC를 비롯한 대만 반도체 산업계에서 갖는 영향력을 보여주는 장면이다.

People in Taiwan from Taipei 101 will always stand behind you, Jensen Huang. pic.twitter.com/NzIwkcnRxA

그러나 엔비디아 이사회는 복귀 요구를 받아들일 움직임을 보이지 않고 있다. 로이터는 사안에 정통한 관계자 3명을 인용해 이사회가 황 전 CEO의 복귀를 검토하지 않고 있다고 보도했다. 이에 앞서 CNBC도 이사회가 복귀를 논의하지 않고 현재 진행 중인 조사에 집중하고 있다고 전했다.

엔비디아는 미국 법률회사 왁텔 립턴을 고용해 황 전 CEO의 행동이 국가안보나 회사의 기밀정보를 위험에 빠뜨렸는지 조사하고 있다. 이사회는 후임 CEO 선임 절차도 진행하고 있다.

투자자들 사이에서도 복귀에 대한 의견은 엇갈리고 있다. 일부 주주들은 황 전 CEO가 엔비디아를 세계 최대 AI 반도체 기업으로 성장시킨 경영 성과와 고객·공급업체와의 긴밀한 관계를 고려해야 한다고 주장한다. 반대로 대형 기관투자자들은 조사가 끝나기 전에 복귀를 결정하면 회사가 추가적인 법적 위험에 노출될 수 있다는 점을 경계하고 있다.

스콧 베선트 미국 재무장관도 엔비디아가 외부에서 새로운 CEO를 영입하고 경영진을 대대적으로 쇄신해야 한다고 주장해 왔다. 이는 트럼프 대통령의 복귀 지지 발언과 차이를 보이는 입장이다.

엔비디아 주가는 이날 3.7% 하락했다. 복귀 요구가 커지는 가운데 황 전 CEO의 거취와 후임 경영진, 관련 조사 결과를 둘러싼 불확실성이 이어지고 있다.

황 전 CEO는 미국 의회의 조사에도 직면해 있다. 오는 12월 첫째 주 복수의 하원 상임위원회가 참여하는 비공개 증언에 나설 가능성이 제기됐으며, 정치권에서는 앨리스 황과의 관계뿐 아니라 엔비디아의 중국 관련 반도체 거래와 수출 통제 문제도 조사 대상으로 삼고 있다.

트럼프 대통령과 실리콘밸리 주요 인사들의 지지로 황 전 CEO의 복귀 요구가 커지고 있지만, 이사회는 조사와 후임 CEO 선임 작업을 이어가고 있다. 황 전 CEO의 복귀 여부는 조사 결과뿐 아니라 이사회의 판단, 기관투자자들의 반응 등에 영향을 받을 것으로 보인다.

items.content:
Altman suggested we all ‘share this memory,’ and said, ‘I think the home tinkering is great.’﻿

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman is once again addressing his controversial comments on PC RAM purchases. “I want to be clear, I want people to have a lot of RAM, I think everybody should be able to buy a lot of RAM for their own computer,” Altman said today. “I think the home tinkering is great.”

The comments were made on stage at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World summit on Monday.

Altman’s remarks on RAM stirred up controversy last month. In an appearance on the Cheeky Pint podcast , Altman said that it’s “quite terrible” for everyone to have RAM in personal computers rather than in data centers. He later followed up on those comments in posts on X earlier this month , saying, “i want you to have so much ram” and saying the original remarks had been “taken out of context.”

AI companies have been buying up the world’s memory supply for data centers, leading to ongoing price hikes on everything from phones to game consoles . Altman commented on supply chain issues, saying OpenAI has “been constrained by different things at different times,” like memory, rack assembly, data center capacity, or “some random component.”

On stage today, Altman went on to say that “a few years ago we started saying the world needs to build a lot more memory supply chain in particular.” He acknowledged how RAM prices have soared over recent months, saying:

“The world did not build out that much, and now we have seen DRAM prices — I don’t know exactly, but maybe they went up 5x, 7x, something like that. I think it would be much better if the world just had a lot of memory. That comment, which I think got misinterpreted, but there is a true part of it, which I will stand by is that, if we’re going to be in this memory supply shortage, then in some sense — whether or not we’ll decide to do it, because I think there are other tradeoffs like people having their own at-home inference — the optimal thing would be, can we share this memory and have it working 100 percent of the time rather than sometimes off in someone’s edge device? Again, optimal use of this limited supply. Maybe it’s not the reason to make the decision but that’s what I was trying to say.”

Altman also commented on Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia’s CEO, saying he “doesn’t know enough” to say if Huang should be reinstated.

items.title: Shareholders sue Intel, its CEO and CFO after stock drops 28.6 percent in one day
items.summary: The PC sales slump "more than offset” AI boom gains, shareholders say.
items.content:
Intel is being sued by shareholders, who are accusing the chipmaker of misleading them about the impact of the PC sales slump that contributed to a drop of 28.6 percent in the price of Intel’s stock on October 30.

The lawsuit ( PDF ), filed on Friday in the San Jose, California, federal court, is seeking class-action certification and lists the City of Southfield Fire and Police Retirement System and “all others similarly situated” as plaintiffs. In addition to Intel, Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan and Intel’s EVP and CFO David Zinsner are listed as defendants.

The plaintiffs claim that Intel made “materially false and misleading statements and omissions” between July 23 and October 29. They are seeking unspecified compensatory damages, plus legal and other associated fees, for shareholders during that period.

In the complaint, the shareholders argue that Intel misled them by failing to disclose: the full impact that the PC market sales slump would have on Intel’s third quarter and beyond; the impact of increasing PC component prices on PC sales for Intel’s OEM and distribution partners; that Intel was dealing with substrate supply constraints that would limit its ability to meet data center CPU demand; and “that any positive impacts to Intel’s business and financial results resulting from data center construction and other aspects of the AI boom were more than offset” by the PC sales slump.

“… statements regarding Intel’s business, operations, financial results, and ability to capitalize on the boom for AI-related infrastructure spending were materially false and misleading when made, and such statements did not accurately reflect Intel’s then-present business and prospects,” the law firm representing the plaintiffs, Robbins Geller Rudman & Dowd LLP, said in a statement issued on Friday.

On October 29, Intel announced what the complaint calls “disastrous” fiscal Q3 earnings. During the quarter, revenue for Intel’s Client Computing and Physical AI Group (CCPG) business declined 5 percent year over year.

At the time, Tan pointed to an “unprecedented memory crunch” and manufacturing supply shortages hurting the PC market.

The next day, Intel’s shares fell 28.6 percent in “the largest single-day price decline for Intel common stock in over 50 years,” the complaint notes.

Intel hasn’t publicly commented on the lawsuit.

items.content:
미국 정부가 중국 기업들이 해외 데이터센터에서 첨단 AI 반도체를 빌려 사용하는 것을 제한하는 새로운 규정을 발표했다. 중국으로의 직접 수출뿐 아니라 해외 GPU의 원격 이용까지 통제하고, 싱가포르와 말레이시아 등 5개국에 대한 첨단 반도체 수출 심사도 강화한다.

미국 상무부 산업안보국(BIS)은 16일(현지시간) 공식 발표 를 통해 첨단 AI 반도체와 서버의 해외 원격 이용을 제한하는 잠정 최종 규정(Interim Final Rule)을 공개했다. 최근 중국 기업의 해외 GPU 임대 규제를 추진하고 있다는 사실이 알려진 데 이어 구체적인 규제 내용이 공식화된 것이다.

이번 규정의 핵심은 해외 데이터센터를 이용한 중국 기업의 AI 모델 훈련까지 수출 통제 대상으로 삼은 것이다. 미국은 그동안 중국에 첨단 AI 반도체를 직접 판매하는 것을 제한했지만, 중국 기업들은 동남아시아 등 다른 국가에 설치된 GPU를 원격으로 임대해 AI 모델을 개발할 수 있었다.

새 규정에 따르면 중국과 러시아 등 미국의 무기 금수 대상국과 마카오에 본사를 둔 기업에 일정 규모 이상의 컴퓨팅 자원을 제공하는 해외 데이터센터는 미국 정부의 수출 허가를 받아야 한다. 규제 대상은 총처리 성능(TPP)이 1200만을 넘는 컴퓨팅 자원으로, 하나의 데이터센터뿐 아니라 네트워크로 연결된 여러 데이터센터의 컴퓨팅 자원도 합산해 판단한다.

중국 기업이 직접 계약하지 않고 제3국의 중개업체를 통해 GPU를 이용하거나, 다른 기업에 AI 모델 훈련을 맡기는 방식도 규제 대상에 포함된다. 데이터센터 운영사와 반도체 수출업체는 고객 기업의 실질적인 소유·지배 관계와 컴퓨팅 자원의 최종 이용 목적을 확인해야 한다.

이미 중국 기업 등에 컴퓨팅 자원을 제공하고 있는 해외 데이터센터도 규정 시행일부터 90일 이내에 허가받아야 서비스를 계속할 수 있다. 허가 없이 서비스를 유지하면 향후 미국의 반도체 수출 제한을 받을 수 있다. 온라인 쇼핑몰과 소셜미디어의 상품·콘텐츠 추천 시스템에만 사용되는 컴퓨팅 자원은 일정 요건을 충족하면 예외로 인정된다.

미국 정부는 이와 별도로 싱가포르, 말레이시아, 태국, 인도네시아, 브라질 등 5개국에 대한 첨단 AI 반도체 수출 허가 요건도 강화했다. 이들 국가가 중국 등 규제 대상국으로 반도체를 우회 공급하는 통로로 활용될 위험이 높다고 판단한 것이다.

이에 따라 5개국으로 첨단 반도체를 수출하거나 재수출할 때 추가 허가가 필요하며, 미국 정부는 거래별로 승인 여부를 심사한다. 미국에 본사를 두거나 미국 기업을 최종 모회사로 둔 기업에 공급하는 반도체는 일정한 신고 요건을 충족하면 추가 허가 의무에서 제외된다.

이번 조치는 최근 엔비디아 AI 반도체의 중국 우회 공급 의혹이 불거지고, 미국 상무부의 수출 통제 관리 부실이 도마 에 오른 직후 발표됐다. 특히 상무부가 규정을 발표했지만, 실제 규정 작성과 발표를 지시한 주체는 재무부와 백악관 국가안보회의(NSC)라는 점이 눈길을 끈다.

최근 스콧 베선트 재무장관은 싱가포르 클라우드 기업 메가스피드에 대한 제재를 상무부가 수개월 동안 미뤄 왔다고 공개적으로 비판했다. 이번에는 재무부와 국가안보회의가 직접 규제 강화를 주도하면서 중국의 첨단 반도체 접근을 차단하는 조치가 공식화됐다.

미국 정부는 이번 규정과 함께 조 바이든 행정부가 2025년 도입한 'AI 확산 규칙(AI Diffusion Rule)'도 공식 폐지했다. 기존 규정은 국가별로 AI 반도체 수출을 차등 제한하는 방식이었으나, 트럼프 행정부는 지난해 집행을 중단하고 새로운 체계로 대체하겠다고 밝힌 바 있다.

이번 규정은 국가별 제한과 함께 실제 컴퓨팅 자원의 이용자와 사용 목적을 확인하는 데 중점을 뒀다. 미국 정부는 해외 데이터센터를 통한 첨단 GPU 접근을 통제함으로써 중국 기업의 최첨단 AI 모델 개발에 필요한 컴퓨팅 자원 확보를 제한하려는 것으로 풀이된다.

미 상무부는 "제3국 데이터센터를 통한 원격 컴퓨팅 방식으로 민감한 미국 기술에 대한 기존 접근 제한을 우회하지 못하도록 설계한 규정"이라고 설명했다.

이번 발표는 도널드 트럼프 미국 대통령이 중국을 방문해 시진핑 국가주석과 정상회담을 갖기 직전에 나왔다. 양국이 AI 반도체 수출 통제를 놓고 대립해 온 가운데 미국이 해외 데이터센터까지 통제 범위를 넓히면서, 중국 기업들의 컴퓨팅 자원 확보 전략과 동남아 데이터센터 사업에도 영향을 미칠 것으로 보인다.

items.title: California state AG sues OpenAI over rogue agent incidents
items.summary: The California lawsuit represents one of the first attempts to hold an AI lab legally accountable for a rogue agent incident
items.content:
OpenAI is facing a new lawsuit from the California Attorney General’s office , alleging that the company’s training practices and lax security present an ongoing danger to the public.

At the center of the case is the July 2026 Hugging Face compromise , in which saw a pre-release model within OpenAI compromise, both companies’ security systems in order to complete a training benchmark. In its official report on the incident , OpenAI called it “an outlier scenario involving a rare and unexpected confluence of events.”

The California lawsuit represents one of the first attempts by a government regulator to hold an AI lab legally accountable for a rogue agent incident, with significant implications for both OpenAI’s competitors and its clients.

The complaint centers around the Hugging Face incident, but also cites similar incidents involving RubyGems , DseWiki , the Wikimedia Foundation and Australian government websites as evidence that the underlying behavior is ongoing.

The complaint also alleges that dozens of other similar incidents have occurred without being disclosed.

“OpenAI has recently sent notices to dozens of additional third parties whose websites or internal systems have been infiltrated by OpenAI agents,” the complaint reads. “In some cases, OpenAI agents were able to access sensitive personally identifiable information, such as employee records containing names, birth dates, addresses, and more. The vast majority of these incidents have not been disclosed or discussed publicly by either OpenAI or by the affected third parties.”

The specific allegation is that OpenAI’s ongoing testing practices represent a public nuisance, on the grounds that the lack of safety controls present an ongoing risk to the public. A secondary claim alleges unfair competition as a result of marketing an unsafe product. If the lawsuit succeeds, OpenAI would face an injunction “to abate the ongoing public nuisance,” leaving broad discretion in the hands of the court.

It’s the first regulatory case targeting OpenAI specifically over rogue agent incidents, although public endangerment claims have been considered by other states. In June, the Florida attorney general sued the company over allegedly harmful effects on users , particularly children and teenagers. In August, the Alabama attorney general launched a probe to investigate deceptive practices related to the breach, but no case has been filed.

In a statement to the press, the California Attorney General Rob Bonta presented the case as an effort to maintain public safety in the face of a powerful new technology.

“OpenAI’s actions escalated real-word cybersecurity risks, threatening the safety, health, and well-being of society. The company knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it,” Bonta said in the statement. “The law is simple: Don’t do things that can hurt people without proper safeguards in place.”

In a statement, OpenAI emphasized the company’s extensive effort to investigate the Hugging Face incident and improve its systems in the aftermath. “This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab,” OpenAI said. “We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged — and will continue to engage — constructively with the Attorney General’s office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry.”

items.title: Uber says hackers stole information on close to 150,000 driver’s licenses during data breach
items.summary: The ridesharing giant said drivers' license information stored by AI cloud company Fireworks AI was stolen during a security incident.
items.content:
Uber is notifying close to 150,000 drivers that their personal and driver’s license information was stolen during an October data breach at one of the company’s tech providers.

In notices filed this week with several U.S. attorneys general, including California and Iowa , the ride-hailing giant said it was notified on October 9 by the provider that hackers broke in and stole internal credentials, which were used to access Uber’s data.

The company said it subsequently began notifying affected drivers that their personal information was stored with the provider.

The stolen data includes affected drivers’ names, addresses, dates of birth, and driver’s license numbers.

TechCrunch has learned that the provider is Fireworks AI, which lets developers access and use open-weight AI models. Fireworks reported a data breach last month in which hackers stole its customers’ information, including billing data and some private AI datasets.

Online productivity startup Notion and AI coding startup Cursor have both confirmed that they had data stolen during the Fireworks hack.

In Uber’s case, the company said it had alerts enabled to detect unauthorized access to its Fireworks environment, but because the hackers used Fireworks’ own internal credentials, “no alerts were triggered.”

When reached for comment, an Uber spokesperson told TechCrunch: “The notices to drivers are in relation to a security incident impacting one of our third-party vendors, Fireworks.ai, which had access to some Uber data,” and deferred our questions to Fireworks.

A spokesperson for Fireworks confirmed that the company identified a security issue involving unauthorized access to some of its systems, which affected customer data, but the spokesperson did not address our questions about the incident.

Fireworks attributed its breach to a financially motivated cybercriminal group whose goals are to sell stolen tokens for accessing large language models, or LLMs. No known cybercriminal group has taken credit for the data theft.

In a notice filed with Oregon’s attorney general, Uber said it notified 149,346 people in total that their information had been taken in the breach at Fireworks.

TechCrunch previously reported that Uber has notified drivers in California, Illinois, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, and South Carolina. We’ve also seen data breach notices filed in Texas and Vermont.

When asked by TechCrunch, Uber’s spokesperson did not say how many drivers are affected by the breach, nor how many drivers it was notifying about the incident.

It’s unclear if the number of affected drivers is expected to rise, and Uber did not respond to a follow-up email sent Monday.

This is Uber’s second known data breach this year. The company reported a security incident at its Uber Freight truck shipping unit, for which an extortion gang took credit for stealing data.

items.content:
Apple’s latest smartwatch introduces AI-powered audio features, redesigned health sensors, and faster charging.﻿

If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

If you’re still sporting an Apple Watch that launched five or so years ago, now is a good time to upgrade. Apple’s latest smartwatch, the 42mm Apple Watch Series 12 with Wi-Fi and GPS connectivity, has dropped to a new all-time low of $329 at Amazon , Best Buy , and Walmart , beating the October Prime Day price by $20. If you prefer a larger size, the 46mm model is on sale for $379 ($70 off) at Amazon , Best Buy , and Walmart , which is also $20 lower than the previous best price.

The Series 12 stands out compared to previous models with its new AI-powered Audio Intelligence features, which are made possible by Apple’s new S11 chip. For example, the watch can alert you when it detects sounds like a doorbell, alarm, or even a baby’s cry, while other upcoming features like Live Rewind and Siri Recap lets you look back at a transcript of the previous 15 seconds of conversation and get a high-level overview of the conversations you had that day. The new chip also makes Siri more responsive, so you can get answers to questions with less waiting around.

It’s not all about AI, though. The Series 12 also features redesigned health sensors that can now track your heart rate every five seconds even when you’re not exercising, which is particularly help if you have a chronic condition and need to keep a closer eye on your heart rate. It also introduces a new readiness score to help you decide how prepared your body is for the day. Other highlights include easier navigation with simple pinch gestures, and faster charging, which helps to make up for the fact that battery life is rated at up to 24 hours on a single charge, just like the previous-generation model. In our testing, the watch went from 20 to 64 percent charge in just 20 minutes, making it relatively easy to top up while showering or getting ready for the day.

items.title: Apple adds ‘face unlock’ to the iPhone Duo, but it’s not Face ID
items.summary: Apple's latest iOS 27.3 developer beta introduces a limited face unlock feature for the iPhone Duo, alongside other improvements.
items.content:
One of the top complaints from tech reviewers about Apple’s new foldable, the iPhone Duo, has been its reliance on Touch ID, a technology that’s been largely replaced by Face ID across the company’s iPhone lineup.

With Monday’s release of iOS 27.3 beta for developers, Apple is addressing that complaint with a new “face unlock” feature that lets iPhone Duo users unlock their phones using the front camera, rather than waiting for a future hardware upgrade.

To be clear, this feature is not Face ID.

Due to hardware constraints, the iPhone Duo shipped without support for Face ID technology primarily because its thin, foldable design doesn’t offer enough space for the TrueDepth sensor array that Face ID requires. A recent report from Bloomberg suggests that the company is working to change that in a future version of the iPhone Duo. In the meantime, the Duo uses Touch ID for unlocking, authentication, and Apple Pay.

The new face unlock feature, however, will allow users to quickly unlock the device using the front camera when the phone is close. It only works if users have recently authenticated with Touch ID or a passcode. Apple notes that Apple Pay and passwords will still require Touch ID, and users will have to authenticate with Touch ID again after 45 minutes of inactivity.

The move is meant to make it easier for people to use the Duo in the way they’re accustomed to, after years of unlocking an iPhone just by looking at it.

Apple isn’t going so far as to allow face unlock to work across the entire device, though, because the technology isn’t as secure as Face ID. The latter uses Apple’s TrueDepth 3D sensing hardware, which includes a flood illuminator and a dot projector that casts over 30,000 invisible infrared dots onto the user’s face to build a unique 3D map of the face. The system combines this map with attention-awareness checks, making it resistant to attempts to fool it with photos or other 2D images.

The software update addresses another complaint by incorporating one of the “hacks” iPhone Duo early adopters were using to force their phone to lock when they shut it. That involved creating a shortcut that would automatically run when the phone was closed. Now, Apple says users can enable this feature directly in Settings, under Display and Brightness.

Alongside the software update, Apple announced that more than 200,000 apps are now optimized for the iPhone Duo, up from over 100,000 earlier this month .

Other new features in this latest software release include an option to ask Siri questions about the content of a webpage, even portions that aren’t visible without scrolling. Apple is also introducing video podcasts in Apple Podcasts in the Apple TV app, catching up with rivals like YouTube and Spotify.

The iOS 27.3 software update is currently available to developers and will soon arrive for public beta testers. It will roll out more broadly to all users after further testing is complete.

items.summary: Apple released betas of iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, and macOS 27.3 today, and the company is using the update to test new per device daily usage limits for some Siri AI and Apple Intelligence features, according to MacRumors. Basic Siri commands and requests will remain free and unlim
items.content:
Frequent users of some Siri AI and Apple Intelligence features will require an iCloud Plus subscription to avoid limits.﻿

Apple released betas of iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, and macOS 27.3 today, and the company is using the update to test new per device daily usage limits for some Siri AI and Apple Intelligence features, according to MacRumors .

Basic Siri commands and requests will remain free and unlimited, but more advanced features that rely on cloud-based processing like generating, cleaning up, or extending images in Photos will be subjected to the daily limits. There are four categories of limited usage, MacRumors reports, including using Siri AI for “multi-step, personal context requests,” image generation and editing tools, automations in Shortcuts that “rely on Apple Foundation Cloud and Cloud Pro Models,” and third-party apps that use those same cloud models.

Apple hasn’t specified exactly how many times those features and tools can be used each day before limits are reached, but they’ll vary based on the task. The company reportedly plans to provide notifications when users are approaching their limit and have finally reached it.

Instead of having to wait until midnight each day for your usage to reset, most of Apple’s existing iCloud Plus plans (excluding the 50GB option) will include higher daily limits at their same price. The $2.99/month 200GB subscription includes 2x the usage, the $9.99/month 2TB plan includes 5x the usage, while the $29.99/month 6TB and $59.99 12TB/month options bump the usage limit to 10x and 20x, respectively. Family members sharing an iCloud Plus subscription will have a shared usage pool that’s used on a first come, first served basis.

Last week Apple updated Logic Pro with an option to “Buy More Usage” for that app’s intelligent assistant through $49.99 Intelligence Usage Packs that are expected to be added to other Apple Creator Studio apps this month, including Pixelmator Pro, Final Cut Pro, Motion, plus Pages, Keynote, and Numbers.

items.title: OpenAI wants to stop deepfakes from overwhelming child abuse tiplines
items.summary: OpenAI is announcing a tool that it says will help child sexual abuse investigators cut through the noise to find harmful material they can act on quickly. At a Monday press briefing in Washington, DC, OpenAI announced a classifier it says can better detect abusive imagery of kid
items.content:
The classifier flagged fewer false positives for humans to review, while getting better at identifying abusive content.

OpenAI is announcing a tool that it says will help child sexual abuse investigators cut through the noise to find harmful material they can act on quickly.

At a Monday press briefing in Washington, DC, OpenAI announced a classifier it says can better detect abusive imagery of kids, including whether it’s AI-generated. It’s also offering free access to vetted organizations, giving developers more guidance on how to detect this type of content, and helping to train law enforcement on how AI can aid their investigations. The news comes as policymakers and others are pushing for more safety restrictions on AI tools, accusing OpenAI and other companies of facilitating harm to children.

In recent years, AI-generated sexual images of children have threatened to overwhelm systems like the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) CyberTipline, which collects and triages reports of child sexual abuse material (CSAM). The CyberTipline received 400,000 generative AI-related reports in 2025, an exponential increase from the 67,000 it received in 2024, and researchers have warned that the influx could make NCMEC’s workload “unmanageable.” The US government has stated that both AI-generated and non-AI-generated CSAM is illegal, and 48 states have laws to address sexually explicit AI deepfakes. But the tools to make them are widely available , and researchers say that a flood of fake images can make it harder to tell when a child is actively experiencing harm.

The influx of AI-generated CSAM reports to NCMEC is “explosive”

North Carolina Attorney General Jeff Jackson, who cochairs the AG Alliance’s AI Task Force , said at OpenAI’s event that the influx of AI-generated CSAM reports to NCMEC is “explosive” — and if they keep going that way, “it is going to mean that we fail in our mission.” Tech companies are facing a range of policy proposals that could require them to take more action against CSAM and other potentially harmful content for kids. The Take It Down Act now requires social media platforms to remove real or AI-generated nonconsensual intimate images within 48 hours, and the newly elected Congress could seek to take stronger action against AI companies like SpaceXSI, whose Grok chatbot went on an undressing spree earlier this year. Last month eight states sued OpenAI for a separate set of alleged harms to children, citing lawsuits alleging ChatGPT encouraged illegal substance use and suicide.

OpenAI says its classifier dramatically cuts down on false positives, flagging 48 percent fewer images, while the images it did identify were twice as likely to contain abusive material. It’s designed to catch abusive AI-generated images produced by a variety of tools, including open-source models and nudifying apps. It’s also the first broadly available CSAM classifier with a specific flag for AI-generated material, said OpenAI’s head of child safety public policy, John Buckley, at the briefing. “It’s important for industry to be able to understand what images may contain a fictional child versus a real child,” Buckley added. “That triage is critical in law enforcement reporting flows.” He also emphasized, however, that laws should recognize the harm of AI-generated CSAM: “It potentially erodes social norms in offending against children, and it’s often found colocated with child sexual abuse imagery of real children,” Buckley said.

OpenAI says its classifier dramatically cuts down on false positives, flagging 48 percent fewer images

OpenAI’s own ChatGPT image generator is designed to deny user requests for CSAM. Now, users who attempt to produce it will be shown a new warning developed with expert guidance to try to encourage them to seek help. A first offense will trigger a 24-hour pause in accessing ChatGPT and warn the user their account could be permanently closed, while offering support resources to combat the behavior. OpenAI says it reports “all instances of CSAM” to NCMEC. In a statement, Buckley explained that the 24-hour pause is based on expert advice for best practices “and international evidence on what works to prevent and respond to CSAM seeking vs CSAM generation.” The point is “to interrupt harmful behavior and direct people toward specialist help to stop it.”

Jackson said that North Carolina and many other states now have laws that cover synthetic CSAM, but that partnering with a tech company like OpenAI to help deter its creation is a fairly novel approach to an emerging issue. “Most of what AGs do is accountability work,” he told reporters at the briefing. “Most of our jurisdiction kicks in after the fact to hold people accountable for harm. But with this, we wanted to see if it was possible to develop a model of working together to prevent that harm. And I would say it’s still basically an experiment.”

items.title: Trump says ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy did not threaten national security
items.summary: Trump contradicted his own government's intelligence officials, who reportedly concluded that Alice Huang is a Chinese spy.
items.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump told reporters on Monday that he does not believe the country’s national security was put at risk as a result of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

“It was not put at risk,” Trump said when asked by reporters in light of his own friendship with Huang. “Our country is now stronger than ever before. And you know, China plays games with us, and we play games with China.”

Trump went on to contradict previous findings from U.S. officials by doubting that Huang’s paramour, former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy.

“He probably shouldn’t have been doing on a personal basis what he did… That’s a different story,” Trump added. “But nobody’s proven that she’s a spy. She may not be a spy.”

Last year, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio reportedly oversaw the production of an internal memo, circulated among top policymakers, which warned that Alice Huang was a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security. Trump was reportedly briefed about these intelligence findings at least twice, including once in May aboard Air Force One, shortly before the former Nvidia CEO joined him on a trip to China. But Trump has maintained that he was not aware of these claims.

The U.S. regulates the exports of Nvidia’s top chips to China as a way of maintaining a competitive advantage. But prior to news of Huang’s affair publicly emerging, both the U.S. and Singaporean governments had been investigating Megaspeed for illegally smuggling Nvidia chips into China. Huang has since stepped down from the role he has had for 33 years at Nvidia after more reporting revealed that he also had affairs with two Nvidia employees, at least one of whom was a direct report.

Given Huang’s importance to Nvidia, some prominent figures in the industry — including Elon Musk, Y Combinator President & CEO Garry Tan, and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney — have signed a public letter calling for Nvidia to reinstate Huang.

“A lot of people are asking Jensen — they think Jensen should go back. That certainly isn’t a bad idea,” Trump said. Referring to former Apple chief executive, Trump added: “I recommended Tim Cook.”

items.title: US moves to cut China’s remote access to AI chips
items.summary: Trump bets China won’t mind US blocking remote access to AI chips.
items.content:
On the heels of the Nvidia scandal , the Trump administration is preparing to crack down on foreign data centers that are fueling China’s advancements in artificial intelligence by allowing remote access to otherwise restricted high-end chips necessary for AI training.

In a summary of the rule change, the Commerce Department said it was closing a loophole that previously allowed foreign rivals like China, Russia, and Iran to bypass export curbs on certain advanced computer chips by instead renting access to those chips from data centers in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil.

US rivals could possibly use that access to train and run advanced AI models “capable of supporting military- and intelligence-related activities that could threaten US national security or foreign policy interests,” the Commerce Department said. Among threats, the US fears rivals could use advanced AI to develop “more effective weapons of mass destruction and advanced conventional weapons, coordinated cyber-espionage and targeted cyber-disruption, algorithmic theft, and weaponized disinformation.”

Now, the rules have been tightened up so much that the South China Morning Post reported that, “as a result, any advanced chips made for a Chinese firm are assumed to be restricted, and factories must ask the US government for a license before shipping them.”

The rule change takes effect 90 days after it’s posted to the Federal Register. Moving forward, companies headquartered in any of those countries deemed to “present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion” to China, Russia, and Iran must apply for a license with strict know-your-customer controls when transferring high volumes of advanced chips. If a license is granted, companies will have to “perform robust due diligence,” submitting monthly reports on transactions that thoroughly detail all parties involved, as well as their parent companies, and the final destination for chips sold.

In a press release Sunday, the Commerce Department described the rule change as “designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries.” An exception was carved out for companies providing computing power “exclusively used for commercial recommender systems.” The Department said it was acting to “prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on US technology to threaten US national security and foreign policy interests.”

Without the intervention, officials fear that China could develop a military or economic edge, The New York Times reported .

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned after admitting to an affair with a woman, Alice Huang, suspected of serving as a Chinese spy . Congress is probing if Alice Huang used her personal relationship with Jensen Huang to help her former company, Megaspeed, become one of Nvidia’s biggest customers, then used that position to smuggle Nvidia’s restricted AI chips into China. China has denied that Alice Huang was a spy, and Megaspeed has denied that smuggling occurred, while launching its own internal probe.

Megaspeed is a Singaporean data center firm whose primary business is cloud computing and AI infrastructure. Prior to the rule change, selling remote access to AI servers to customers in China was perfectly legal, NYT noted. But now, the Commerce Department has given firms like Megaspeed 90 days to either obtain licenses or face future export restrictions.

Whether or not to add more chip curbs has been a polarizing debate in the Trump administration. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent reportedly butted heads with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. When the Megaspeed news broke, Bessent pushed for curbs, but Lutnick reportedly appeared “too cozy” with Nvidia to move. Instead, Lutnick initially favored looser controls that Nvidia claimed would ensure global dominance of US technology. (A Commerce Department spokesperson told NYT that Bessent has never confronted Lutnick over his handling of Megaspeed.)

Any companies found violating the rules could face a “range of consequences,” the Commerce Department said after reportedly bending to Bessent’s pressure campaign. Those include possibly facing new import restrictions, stricter license requirements, downgrading their status in the US export control regime, or other changes to their company’s or their base country’s entity-list designations.

Although the summary of the rule change said that “Commerce will be actively monitoring for countries that tolerate evasion” of the anti-diversion policy, it’s unclear how aggressively the Commerce Department might enforce the rule, NYT noted.

Bessent has publicly criticized Lutnick for failing to sanction Megaspeed, and NYT reported that ultimately, enforcement of the stricter rules—which Bessent helped draft—“would be up to the Commerce Department.”

“The real story here should be: Did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies?” Bessent said on a CNBC appearance. “I think it’s important that anyone at the company there be held accountable for that.”

There’s even a push to oust Lutnick over his position on chips, but The Guardian reported that Donald Trump confirmed he has no plans to replace the AI industry-friendly commerce secretary. On Monday, Trump told reporters that Lutnick was right to delay blacklisting Megaspeed, because “if you didn’t delay it… you could have a blow-up with China.”

At the press gaggle, Trump aligned with China in saying that there’s no evidence yet that Alice Huang was a spy. He also joined a band of prominent tech leaders calling for Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia, saying that it wasn’t a “bad idea.”

“Nobody’s proven that she’s a spy,” Trump said. “She may not be a spy.”

items.title: The open-source movement wants Jensen Huang back
items.summary: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here. On Friday, a petition to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia began circulating on social media, and by Monday it listed some notable signa
items.content:
On Friday, a petition to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia began circulating on social media, and by Monday it listed some notable signatories, including Elon Musk and several influential Nvidia researchers. But comb through the more than 115,000 names and you’ll notice a significant faction of Huang’s supporters—higher-ups from Hugging Face, a hub for sharing AI models, and venture capital firms Andreessen Horowitz and Sequoia Capital—come from a particular slice of the tech world.

These names have a vested interest in the development of open-source AI, models that, unlike ChatGPT or Claude, can be downloaded and run independent of large tech companies. Supporters of such models say that concentrating AI in the hands of a few powerful companies will leave everyone else worse off (a concern that wouldn’t sound out of place among the AI industry's critics on the left, if so many open-source advocates weren’t also venture capitalists who stand to profit when startups can build on cheaper AI without paying Big Tech).

Huang had become a sort of ringleader for those who defend open source to policymakers against concerns that such models come with no guardrails and cede AI leadership to China, where the most powerful and popular open-source models are created. They now want their most influential voice returned to his post.

But it’s not just Huang’s extramarital affairs that threaten his (and Nvidia’s) credibility as an advocate for open-source AI. New research into China’s startups using Nvidia’s chips, and a new rule from the US Department of Commerce announced Monday, could deal a blow to both the movement’s reputation and its technical progress.

On Thursday, the day Huang resigned, ex-OpenAI researcher Will DePue published findings online suggesting that China’s AI companies had far more access to Nvidia’s advanced Blackwell chips than previously estimated. China is banned from accessing Nvidia’s most cutting-edge chips to help protect America’s AI lead.

It’s unclear how they would have gained access to the chips. DePue claims the results were verified by senior researchers at OpenAI and Anthropic, but an independent analysis has not confirmed the results. (DePue did not respond to a request for an interview. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.)

The findings do not establish that Nvidia helped Chinese companies obtain the chips, and the broader problem of chip smuggling was already known to extend well beyond Nvidia’s control.

But in suggesting that Nvidia may have profited from the rise of Chinese AI startups, whose models are increasingly being used by American companies instead of domestic alternatives, the findings do leave Huang in an awkward position. He has championed open-source AI as a way to strengthen American technological leadership. “Without open source, startups can’t thrive, university researchers can’t do research, you can’t teach AI, scientists can’t use AI,” he said last December during a talk about helping the US win the AI race against China.

It also makes the idea of reinstating Huang even more of a long shot. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent even said last week that Nvidia should not consider someone from inside the company to replace him. The new findings lower Huang’s chances further.

What happens next? Nvidia announced in September it would acquire Hugging Face for nearly $13 billion. Its support for open source also serves a straightforward financial interest: The more businesses that build their own models instead of forking over money to Anthropic and OpenAI, the more chips Nvidia can sell.

But a new rule from the US Department of Commerce could mean the models popular on Hugging Face will soon stop getting smarter. The rule aims to prevent Chinese companies from training models on Nvidia chips that they can’t own directly, but that they can access remotely in data centers in countries like Malaysia—a workaround that has helped China’s open-source models get so good.

The open-source world rallied around Huang because of his influence on policymakers. That was important, since the rise of China’s open-source models has splintered some in Trump’s orbit. If Huang is out, who is next?

Ten years after AlphaGo’s match against Go champion Lee Sedol, today’s AI still isn’t tapping into the machinery that made that win possible.

items.title: The iPhone Duo Is Getting a Limited Version of Face ID
items.summary: Originally launching only with Touch ID, Apple’s folding phone now borrows a feature from the new HomeView and can recognize your mug, but it’s likely not as secure as Face ID.
items.content:
Apple's most expensive smartphone—the iPhone Duo —lacks one of the company's hallmark features: Face ID . The folding phone is already jam-packed with a hinge and multiple display layers, leaving no room for the TrueDepth sensor required for biometric face authentication. The Duo relies on Touch ID instead .

That's changing now in a software update. On Monday, Apple announced that it's bringing facial recognition to the iPhone Duo as part of the iOS 27.3 update. But since it can't rely on the tried-and-true Face ID system without those crucial components, it's borrowing the feature from the company's recently launched smart display, the HomeView .

The HomeView personalizes the display content for up to six people in a household, with its camera recognizing people who step in front of it (it also uses voice data for recognition when someone asks Siri a command). This “person recognition” technology is protected by the Secure Exclave—different from the Secure Enclave chip that houses Face ID data—a memory-protected space in Apple's A20 Pro processor. As WIRED's Lily Hay Newman writes , it's still not as comprehensive as Face ID, and could be more susceptible to attacks.

At launch, the iPhone Duo relied on Touch ID for biometric authentication.

Rumors abound that Apple is racing to add proper Face ID to the second-generation iPhone Duo. Still, tight development cycles might mean the feature may not arrive until the third generation in 2028. That also points to limitations in the Duo's new facial recognition tech.

You cannot use it to authenticate payments or unlock sensitive content, like your banking app. You'll still need your thumbprint or passcode to approve Apple Wallet purchases. Instead, it's designed to unlock the foldable without tapping a finger on the Touch ID sensor. There is also a time-based limitation. For face recognition to work, it needs a recent Touch ID or passcode authentication within a 45-minute window. This capability is also restricted to the front screen and camera—it doesn't work if the iPhone Duo is unfolded. Also in iOS 27.3, Apple has a new toggle that lets you lock your iPhone Duo when you close it.

Google's newer Pixel folding phones are the only ones on the US market with secure facial authentication, though it's not as effective in the dark as Apple's Face ID. Samsung's facial biometrics on its Galaxy phones aren't strong enough to protect sensitive content and are largely used to unlock the device.

Apple’s willingness to roll out a watered-down version of Face ID is a rare compromise for the company—and shows just how much of a friction point Touch ID has become for Duo owners.

items.title: Software is breaking down at a systemic level
items.summary: Article URL: https://www.breck-mckye.com/blog/2026/11/software-is-breaking-down-at-a-systemic-level/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50520866 Points: 249 # Comments: 136
items.content:
Software hasn’t been working too well lately, has it?

This weekend we saw the double-whammy of a 2 day global Microsoft outage, then an FAA ground-stop that halted all flights in the United States.

Can you believe it’s only been four weeks since the PHP2Shell vulnerability? A critical exploit in PHP, powering an estimated 70% of the world’s websites, with sites taken completely offline as engineers frantically patched their systems.

And then there was the eMudhra fiasco , where thousands of SSL certificates - the way we secure HTTPS websites and internet traffic - were compromised by a private key so weak, it was almost comical.

It’s like 2026 has been a year of hacks, outages, vulnerabilities and IT panics. What exactly is going on here?

You might be tempted to blame AI, and you wouldn’t be completely wrong. Artificial intelligence models are definitely a part of this. Even if companies like Microsoft don’t divulge whether broken systems were built with AI, we do know that hackers and researchers can now use AI technology to find complicated exploits in a matter of hours.

I work with AI heavily in my job. It’s tremendously powerful. It’s also corrosive if used unwisely.

But AI is both a cause and a symptom of the problem here. What we are seeing is software breaking down at a systemic level. This problem is insidious because it is not only the software itself that is broken, but the entire way we’ve come to build it.

Look at the recent crises in software reliability and you’ll notice they don’t share immediate causes - that we know of - yet they look uncannily similar to each other.

The Microsoft outage likely emerged from a network configuration failure that stopped MS datacenters communicating with each other. Exactly what happened next remains confidential, but it seems to have triggered a cascading failure where no service could be restored into a valid state long enough to bear traffic.

Reddit and Bluesky speculated that even MSFT engineers had no real handle on the complexity of this outage.

Microsoft have faced increasing criticism for the (un)reliability of their Azure platform. Back in March, ex-MSFT engineer Axel Rischin published this scathing criticism :

Microsoft rushed Azure out of the gates under intense competitive pressure. Corners were cut. Fundamental principles of reliability and operational simplicity were quietly abandoned.

Instead of going back to the drawing board to tackle the growing technical debt, Microsoft relied on quick fixes: layers of automation running mitigation scripts, a growing team of on-call staff, and, when automation was not enough, manual repairs.

His article depicts a highly complex system made of low quality parts, where nobody can make sense of the whole picture.

On October 21st, security research firm Wiz proudly shared an exploit that could execute arbitrary code on any PHP website . Called PHP2Shell, Wiz trumpeted the power of AI tools to achieve exploits far beyond the skills of human attackers.

It turns out the PHP runtime had hidden several complex memory bookkeeping bugs for over a decade. PHP is used extensively in e-commerce and most famously in WordPress, which was once the go-to for cheaply building simple websites.

The PHP2Shell writeup depicts an internet dependent on a long chain of dependencies, hiding vulnerabilities too complex for any human to identify.

Most people outside of tech won’t have heard of this, but back in May we faced a crisis when an attacker compromised some important packages in the JavaScript ecosystem (NPM).

These packages used GitHub Actions to perform Continuous Integration (CI) - automated tests, releases, etc. - and had a crucial misconfiguration where anyone who forked their projects could insert compromised code back upstream.

When the next upstream CI build ran, it would retrieve libraries from a cache. The JavaScript package manager, NPM, allows these libraries to include scripts. They’re intended for housekeeping tasks, but here, they were used to hijack the projects’ secret tokens.

The JavaScript ecosystem has long been criticised for poor security. NPM projects are complicated chains of dependencies calling dependencies calling dependencies.

Any dependency may carry scripts. Any dependency author was just one slip away from allowing their code to be compromised - all they had to do was copy-paste the wrong code.

In other words: a highly complex system made of low quality parts, where a single error can compromise everything.

It wasn’t always like this. Only 12 years ago, tech was a different industry.

Building software was hard . Computer programs comprise millions of tiny instructions, and turning these into a workable system is like constructing a watch by hand, with hundreds of interacting components. Except, unlike a watch, each computer program must do something completely new and different.

It was the most fun I’d had as an adult. It was as much an art as a science. You had to be able to hold everything in your head at once: visualise how all the tiny parts could be orchestrated into a cohesive whole. I recommend anyone the adventure of writing a computer program by hand.

But, it was less fun if you were a manager. Not many people can write computer programs well, and it’s very hard to scale human beings. Getting them to communicate without misunderstandings is hard. Many projects failed. You can find programmers who know how to manage the complexity, but they want to be paid lots of money.

Different movements attempted to solve the core problem. Some people thought that software development practices could help, like if you turned programming into highly structured templates of “best practices”. Or if you used management styles like SCRUM. But they only ever helped so much.

About ten years ago, two small revolutions happened in our industry, whilst the rest of the world paid little attention. They were cloud computing, and open source libraries.

items.title: Sam Altman on Nvidia without Jensen Huang: the industry will be ‘fine’
items.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman acknowledged the special role Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has played in the AI boom, but ultimately thinks the industry will be “fine” without him at the helm.
items.content:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says the AI industry will be “fine” without Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at the helm, even as he acknowledged the special role Huang has played in the AI boom.

Huang resigned last week from Nvidia after admitting to having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

Altman made his first public comments about Huang’s departure on Monday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley and the World event, where he also discussed topics ranging from data center pushback to recursive self-improvement.

Numerous executives and members of the AI industry have argued for Nvidia to reinstate Huang, including Elon Musk and Epic Games chief executive Tim Sweeney, who were among the signatories in a public letter. Many fear that Huang’s departure may cause Nvidia to rethink the enormous financial risks it has taken that have fueled the AI boom.

Huang is also reportedly setting up a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for his return.

When asked whether he thought Huang should return to the company, Altman said: “I don’t think I know enough to answer that question.”

He expressed empathy for Huang’s situation, citing his own ousting from OpenAI in 2023 after board members accused him of withholding information.

“It’s hard to imagine what the AI revolution without Jensen and the company he has built,” Altman said, adding that he sees Huang as a hero, and that “heroes have flaws.”

OpenAI and Nvidia have had a close relationship for the last decade, one that has evolved from a simple chip supplier-customer relationship into a potentially circular financing arrangement, in which Nvidia’s money helps fund purchases of its own chips. Most recently, Nvidia agreed to provide a guarantee of up to $105 billion backing OpenAI’s Ohio data center project. That’s just one of many such circular deals Nvidia has made to bankroll the AI boom while fueling demand for its own chips.

Altman said he’s not worried that the Bank of Nvidia will dry up.

“Nvidia is, like, a behemoth of a company,” he said. “I think people still trust their guarantees very much.”

Altman acknowledged the “ambition” Huang brought to the industry, the scale of which “has been quite important.” But he didn’t go so far as to agree with the many who worry about ripple effects from Huang’s departure.

“I think there’s so much demand, and it’s so clear that AI is real, and people want to use it, and the revenues and demand are growing so strongly that I think the industry will be fine,” Altman said. “But again, I think Jensen has played this extremely special and valuable role as someone to really drive things forward with great ambition.”

items.title: FBI says Artex AI open-source hacking tool used to breach networks in ‘under three hours’
items.summary: The FBI says that the open-source hacking tool was used in cyberattacks targeting a U.S. IT giant and the South Korean financial industry.
items.content:
The FBI is warning that hackers are relying on autonomous AI hacking tools to launch cyberattacks across the U.S. and globally. The campaigns include a widespread hack of customers of American IT company ConnectWise and across South Korea’s financial industry.

In its latest flash cybersecurity advisory , the FBI says hackers have targeted several industries in recent months, including financial services, government, tech, defense, phone and internet companies, and law firms, using open-source tools like Artex to carry out autonomous-driven cyberattacks.

Artex is one of several open-source AI-powered penetration testing platforms, a category of software built to probe a network’s defenses. Hackers can connect Artex to hosted frontier large language models (LLMs) like those from Anthropic and OpenAI, as well as to open-source models and non-U.S. models. The FBI says Artex intrusions can be “noisy,” meaning they generate reams of traffic and data that may trigger a targeted company’s defensive alerts. But the tools allow hackers to move at speeds that makes it far more harder for human defenders to keep up.

In some cases, Artex-linked attacks can move from targeting a system to active compromise “in under three hours.”

The FBI’s warning comes as AI-powered hacks are escalating, particularly by finding easy-to-find security flaws and breaking into companies with relative ease.

Oftentimes, Artex will rely on rapidly scanning a victim’s network to look for signs of weakness, and then exploit simple security bugs, such as weak protections and exposed or stolen passwords to gain a foothold. From there, Artex allows the hacker to spread across the network for databases, mailboxes, and other sensitive information.

The FBI’s advisory noted that Artex has been used in several cyberattacks since the tool’s first public debut in July. Artex was used to hack a number of South Korean financial institutions, blamed in large part on weak cybersecurity defenses and lacking protections, such as multi-factor authentication. The attacks allowed hackers to steal the personal data of at least 68,000 people.

The FBI confirmed earlier findings from Microsoft that hackers also used Artex to break into IT management giant ConnectWise and gain access to the Microsoft 365 cloud environments of at least 2,250 of its customers.

The hackers, who Microsoft says are likely Chinese, used the tool to steal data from affected ConnectWise customers.

A spokesperson for ConnectWise did not respond to a request for comment about the FBI’s claim.

Cybersecurity company Barracuda also disclosed that it was breached as part of an Artex-linked attack by financially motivated criminals, in which the tool found an exposed credential belonging to a third-party service that Barracuda had not revoked when it ended work with the vendor. That access allowed the hackers to access stores of credentials used by Barracuda to collect data from its customers’ systems. Barracuda said it couldn’t rule out access, as its logs were not detailed enough, and chose to “assume the worst” and changed all of its customer credentials.

“Defenders who rely on spotting malicious activity and then responding to it will often arrive after the attacker has finished,” wrote Barracuda’s chief information security officer Arve Kjoelen.

A spokesperson for Barracuda told TechCrunch that the company “directly notified and advised a minority of XDR customers to revoke and recreate integration credentials,” but did not specify how many customers.

After Artex was used in cyberattacks, the tool’s developer made the software closed-source to prevent further attacks. But the FBI says the previous open-source version continues to circulate and remains “widely accessible” for use in cyberattacks.

It’s not only companies and targeted victims that have been compromised as a result of weakened security exploited by AI tools; the tools themselves have been exposed as well, potentially allowing outsiders to access powerful hacking capabilities. Last week, researchers found hundreds of publicly exposed Artex systems online , which had been placed on the internet without a password, likely by mistake or misconfiguration — including the Artex system that was used to target South Korea.

items.title: Jordan Belfort’s new AI voice startup, Tone, wants to sell like the ‘Wolf of Wall Street’
items.summary: Belfort claims his AI sales voice can already close deals almost as well as the best human salespeople, and he thinks it will catch up in a year.
items.content:
Years ago, as questions mounted about WeWork’s soaring valuation, I sat down with co-founder Adam Neumann. We were negotiating a stage interview, and he asked to meet me twice in the weeks leading up to it, once at a WeWork in San Francisco and again at his office in New York.

I knew full well that the numbers that SoftBank in particular had assigned to WeWork made little sense , but I came away understanding why investors wanted to throw in their lot with him.

It’s similarly easy to understand why people are enchanted by Jordan Belfort, the self-proclaimed “Wolf of Wall Street.” Belfort famously pleaded guilty in 1999 to securities fraud and money laundering tied to Stratton Oakmont, the Long Island brokerage where salespeople pushed penny stocks in pump-and-dump schemes while Belfort acquired a Southampton mansion, a 167-foot yacht, and at least one helicopter. (He destroyed the latter two while high on Quaaludes and cocaine, as depicted in Martin Scorsese’s famous adaptation of Belfort’s autobiography, “The Wolf of Wall Street.”)

You might think someone who spent 22 months in prison and was ordered to pay $110.4 million in restitution to 1,513 victims wouldn’t get another shake. The victims ultimately received “far less” than they were owed, TMZ reported in July , noting that Belfort completed his court-ordered restitution obligations in late April of this year.

But Belfort, whose energy has a galvanizing quality, keeps resurfacing, including in recent years as a Miami-based sales consultant and one-time host of crypto workshops at his Miami Beach home. (A New York Times reporter attended a weekend workshop several years ago where the price of admission was one bitcoin or its equivalent value at the time of $40,000.)

Now, he is moving into the intersection of what he knows best — sales — and the hottest trend on the planet, AI, building out a voice-based AI platform. The secret sauce is that it imbues its voices with the kind of tonality that wins deals, he says, for example, by phrasing declarative statements as questions (which “builds engagement”) and even whispering at times (which “implies scarcity of information”).

Belfort says the platform, called Tone , is already being used by companies that have more sales leads than their human teams can handle. Now, in a move that could also help expand its training data, Tone is launching a self-service platform for content creators and authors who want to turn their books into “expressive AI-generated narration.” Users can select from Tone’s AI voices or, as a voice-cloning feature rolls out, create a clone of their own voice.

It’s easy to argue the market is already saturated with AI voice startups and technologies, and Tone comes with added risk: Belfort’s co-founder in the business is longtime investor Shervin Pishevar, who has a controversial past of his own. We also can’t independently verify that the technology works as described (neither co-founder is an engineer).

But if my time with Neumann taught me anything, it’s that doubts about the numbers rarely get in the way of a good pitch. When Belfort looks for investors to back him in this new venture, finding believers won’t be too hard.

Here is part of our conversation, edited for length and clarity. What have you built?

It’s a very unique way of going about building a voice, and it stems from a system of influence and persuasion I’ve been teaching since the late 1980s. It’s not just what you say, but how you say it. When you’re not in person, body language collapses into tonality. There are about 15 very powerful tonalities that people use all the time. The phrase I invented for this was “goal-oriented communication.” If I’m trying to be perceived as an expert, I apply tonality strategically.

Is this effectively trained on you?

It started that way. As a non-engineer, I went to first principles: How would I teach a human to do this? One tonality at a time. I have 30 years of super high-quality data , and I started teaching the model. It was a breakthrough moment, because it not only sounded exactly like me, it had nailed the tonality. Then I taught it a second one, and then how to link them. The key to all of this is data. Even the littlest bit of corrupt data dramatically negates the progress you’ve made.

How did you and Shervin Pishevar come together?

Shervin and I have been personal friends for a long time, and we were out for dinner one night. I had been pitched by an AI company that said it had an AI that could do selling. I listened to it. It was awful. But it put the idea in my head. I thought I was just going to teach models how to sell, but I couldn’t find a voice that was good enough. Necessity is the mother of invention, so we built our own.

Who are your customers, and how do they use it?

We have law firms and health insurance companies. We do a lot in polling and automobiles. It will take you through an entire health insurance sale. It asks qualifying questions, like what type of insurance you want, your budget, your ages. Then it chooses a plan and explains the features and benefits. Our latency is like 600 milliseconds. If the payment is too high, it’ll say it can bring the payment down and explain how to raise your deductible. If you don’t like the plan, it swaps you to a different one. It does literally the whole entire sale.

How does the AI handle a sales call that goes off script?

It never says “That’s a great question,” unless it really is. I hate that. It’s so ingratiating. In any sale there’s a happy path, how we’d want the perfect conversation to go, and every last word can be mapped out. But people have questions and concerns, and they take you off the straight line. So the trick is a model that can carry that perfect conversation, handle anything thrown at it, answer elegantly and return to the straight line, without breaking rapport and without hallucinating — or, as a salesperson, lying. We’ve trained the model to do that.

items.summary: OpenAI will embed six Apollo Research evaluators to investigate whether its AI models engage in subversive behavior, but restrictions on access and disclosure raise questions about their independence.
items.content:
OpenAI will embed safety evaluators from Apollo Research, Goodfire, METR, and Transluce in its organization as part of a pilot, OpenAI said Monday. The news follows a series of safety incidents, including one in which an OpenAI agent swarm broke out of its sandbox and hacked into Hugging Face during cybersecurity testing. Many AI safety researchers, including from Apollo, have argued such an event might have been avoided if outside evaluators had been embedded within OpenAI to monitor its safety testing.

OpenAI said the efforts support its commitments to rely on independent assessments of safety controls under the White House Accord on Super Intelligence. The pilots will begin at different points, with Apollo’s beginning this week, according to OpenAI.

The idea of embedding evaluators into frontier AI labs first came from Anthropic , which last month started to give METR researchers employee-level access to its systems. Until recently, AI companies have only brought in outside reviewers to test models after post-training and shortly before public release. Evaluators say this is insufficient because it doesn’t allow them to test for misaligned behaviors like scheming during training or to monitor internal deployment use cases that could still pose a threat.

The work with each third-party firm differs in scope. The pilot with OpenAI and Apollo will focus on investigating whether models attempt to subvert their own or their successors’ alignment or control mechanisms. In other words, they’ll be on the lookout for whether AI models try to undermine the safety rules and safeguards designed to keep them, or future versions of themselves, under human control. OpenAI recently published findings that while training GPT-5.6 Sol, it began leaving instructions for future versions of itself telling them to conceal mistakes and misaligned behavior from the user.

Per Apollo, the pilot will examine whether training incentivizes subversion; whether evaluations can elicit subversion; whether subversion occurs during internal deployment; and whether reasoning relevant to subversion would be detectable. These risks are becoming increasingly important to monitor as AI models grow more capable of acting autonomously and deceiving humans. Apollo’s previous research with OpenAI found that models can behave differently when they know they’re being tested and tend to prioritize what evaluators want to see over users’ actual institutions.

Goodfire will embed researchers who specialize in understanding how AI models work internally. Using its interpretability platform, the firm will help OpenAI monitor training runs, fix undesired behavior, and improve alignment, per the company. Goodfire says it will publish findings, though its primary audience will be OpenAI’s own researchers.

With METR, OpenAI plans to perform two evaluations: one that looks for unintended or dangerous behavior in the model itself, including problems OpenAI’s own tests might have missed, and another that tests whether OpenAI’s systems are capable of catching that behavior. For the first evaluation, METR will largely decide for itself what to investigate and how to test the model. OpenAI and METR have not yet come to a decision on the scope of the second assessment, according to OpenAI.

Transluce, meanwhile, will examine whether OpenAI’s post-training safety evaluations themselves are good enough. The organizations also planning to test in 2027 how OpenAI uses its safety tests to decide whether a model is safe enough to release.

At a time when the independence of third-party evaluations is under scrutiny, it’s worth noting that Apollo and Goodfire are both receiving financial compensation for their evaluations. METR and Transluce aren’t, but they may accept compute or API credits.

Apollo, which published the most detailed account of its agreement with OpenAI, offers a closer look at the scope and limitations of these evaluations.

Many in the AI safety community have warned that AI labs might try to stymy evaluators’ independence, especially if outsiders find unflattering evidence that labs would rather keep hidden. Apollo says an essential part of the pilot is OpenAI’s agreement that the firm can publicly explain the conditions and limitations of its work.

Still, there are areas where Apollo believes its access to OpenAI’s systems is lacking. For a truly independent evaluation of the company’s AI models, Apollo says it needs true employee-level access to OpenAI’s systems, including “all data, records and documentation relevant to their assessment even if a developer was trying to hide unfavorable information.” Getting access to all data, including training data and evaluation logs which companies are loathe to show to outsiders, is important for, say, checking a company’s claims about how a model performed or determining when certain concerning behavior emerged.

In previous coverage, John Steidley, chief of staff at Palisade Research, told TechCrunch that it’s important to see this data in order to assess whether a model was trained to perform well on a “shutdown resistance benchmark.”

In OpenAI’s first pilot, the AI lab is providing Apollo with access to only the information required to assess whether the models engage in subversion attempts. This includes “relevant training code and datasets, reinforcement-learning rollouts with available reasoning traces and rewards, and the ability to query intermediate model checkpoints.”

The scope of access will be limited to “only the agreed claims and only for the specific models and time periods agreed for the assessment,” Apollo says. OpenAI still reserves the right to withhold certain information within that scope if it deems it necessary because of technical infeasibility, security risks, or IP protection. The company agreed not to withhold information simply because it is unfavorable.

items.title: OpenAI releases a new image classifier and ChatGPT warnings to combat CSAM
items.summary: ChatGPT will ban an account trying to access CSAM content for 24 hours as a warning
items.content:
OpenAI today announced new tools to combat child sexual abuse material (CSAM) amid growing safety concerns around the use of AI tools. These features include a new image classifier to detect CSAM, warnings and temporary blocks to prevent users from creating or accessing content that sexualizes children, a new guideline for developers, and a set of tools for law enforcement.

The company unveiled a new image classifier that can detect CSAM images, including the ones generated by AI. OpenAI is giving select companies access to its classifier through its API at no cost. The tool looks for visual signs of abuse in images not seen before and assigns a score that can give an indicative direction to reviewers about dealing with CSAM.

OpenAI said that it developed this classifier with the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC), and it is working with Tech Coalition and ROOST to share access to the tool. In its early testing with partners, the AI company found that the classifier flags 48% fewer images while finding the same number of abusive images, reducing the work of reviewers. Plus, images flagged by the classifier are twice as likely to be abusive images.

What’s more, the company is adding new warning screens in ChatGPT to prevent users from accessing material that sexualizes children. ChatGPT will show an alert to users attempting such prompts, direct users towards specialized support to stop harmful behaviour, and also suspend the account for 24 hours as a warning. The app already blocks CSAM content and requests related to it. It said that repeated offences could lead to the account being removed permanently.

OpenAI noted that it formed the message and guidelines around this behavior with organizations and researchers, including Protect Children , the Lucy Faithfull Foundation , and Joel Scanlan at the University of Tasmania, who independently evaluated a trial of deterrent messages.

The company is also publishing guidelines for developers using OpenAI tools to prevent, detect, and help users report CSAM content. It said that in early testing, the guidelines have helped a number of developers adopt child safety tooling and register to report CSAM to NCMEC. OpenAI is also equipping law enforcement dealing with child safety with AI-powered features like dedicated plugins, investigative tools, and complex data analysis, with access managed by program administrators. It is also providing training to investigators along with a field guide on how to use AI.

OpenAI has had several lawsuits against the company blaming its technology for harming users, especially children. Saftey-focused nonprofit Common Sense Media labeled OpenAI’s tech as “unacceptable risk” for teens. Other AI chatbots — specifically Grok — have been used to create nonconsensual sexualized imagery, including of children .

The AI startup had made changes in the last 12 months to its technology including releasing a safety blueprint , updating content guidelines to bar inappropritate content , retuning its model to prevent them from generating harmful content , and releasing a special version of ChatGPT for teens .

items.title: Instagram now lets creators add Amazon affiliate links in reels and feed posts
items.summary: While creators have long shared Amazon affiliate links through stories, DMs, and their bios, the new integration brings them to new parts of the app.
items.content:
Instagram announced on Monday that it’s launching an integration that will give creators a new way to earn by adding Amazon affiliate links directly in reels and feed posts. Creators can add up to 30 products per reel or 20 per feed post, which makes it possible for them to earn from multiple products through one piece of content.

While creators have long shared Amazon affiliate links through stories, DMs, and their bios, the new integration brings them to new parts of the app. The Meta-owned company told TechCrunch in an email that it has seen product links directly on creators’ reels and posts draw about twice as many clicks as the links in their bio.

By allowing creators to embed multiple product links directly in Reels and feed posts, the platform is expanding their opportunities to monetize content, while also giving them more flexibility in how they share recommendations. The change also strengthens the platform’s appeal to creators, as it continues to compete with rivals like TikTok and YouTube for their attention and content.

Instagram says adding products and affiliate links is free, and that it doesn’t take a commission on purchases or charge transaction fees.

Eligible creators can now connect their Instagram and Amazon Influencer accounts through the Monetization section of their Professional Dashboard. Once connected, Instagram automatically adds affiliate links when creators tag Amazon products in their content, with links directing viewers to the Amazon Shopping app. Connected affiliates also unlock image previews for their links, making it easier for viewers to recognize the products.

When creators connect their Amazon Associates account to Instagram, affiliate attribution is automatically applied to any Amazon product they add, even when they paste a regular product link, which wasn’t the case before, as they were required to add an affiliate URL.

Instagram says creators can also see each product’s estimated commission rate before adding it to a post or reel, with commissions continuing to be paid out by Amazon.

The new integration marks another step in Instagram’s efforts to expand its monetization tools while also making affiliate marketing more accessible for creators on its platform.
